chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, and Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, both together, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I asked Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) about a man who married a woman secretly from her family, and she was in her family's house, and he intended to divorce her, but he could not reach her to know her menstruation when she menstruates, nor her purity when she is pure. He (peace be upon him) said: 'This is like the absentee from his family; he divorces her by the new moons and the months.'

I said, 'What is your view if he can reach her at times, and at times he cannot reach her, so he knows her state? How should he divorce her?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'When a month passes for him during which he cannot reach her, he divorces her when he looks at the first day of the next month, with witnesses, and he writes down the month in which he divorces her, and makes two men witness her divorce. When three months have passed, she is irrevocably divorced from him, and he is a suitor among suitors, and upon him is her maintenance during those three months in which she observes her waiting period.'

key_terms.بَانَتْ مِنْهُ: She is irrevocably divorced from him
key_terms.غُرَّةُ الشَّهْرِ: The first day of the month

ai.seo_question: How does a husband divorce his wife if he cannot observe her menstruation due to separation?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi addresses the fiqh of 'talaq al-mu'allaq' (conditional or delayed divorce) for couples in separation, distinguishing between a fully absent husband and one with intermittent access. It establishes a rigorous evidentiary standard requiring written records and two witnesses to count months based on lunar cycles, ensuring the wife's 'iddah' (waiting period) is accurately observed before the final separation. This ruling highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on preventing ambiguity in marital status when physical cohabitation is irregular.

en.hubeali: Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Ahmad Bin Muhammad, and Ali Bin Ibrahim, form his father, both together from Ibn Mahboub, from Abdul Raham Bin Al Hajjaj who said,

‘I asked Abu Al-Hassan<sup>asws</sup> about a man who married a woman secretly from her family and she was in the house of her family, and had intended to divorce her, and he could not go to her. So he knew her menstruation when she menstruated, and did not know of her purity when she was pure. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘This is like the absentee from his wife. He divorces her by the new-moons and the months’.

I said, ‘What is your<sup>asws</sup> view if he could sometimes go to her and sometimes he could not go to her, so he would know of her state, how should he divorce her?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘When a month passes by for him, not being able to go to her in it, he can divorce her by looking at the onset of the month, with witnesses, and he writes down the month in which he divorces her, and keeps two men as witnesses upon his divorcing her. So when three months pass by, so she is irrevocably divorced from him, and he is a proposer from the proposers, and upon him is her expenses in the third month which she had her waiting period in’.
en.sarwar: 1. Muhammad ibn Yahya has narrated from Ahmad ibn Muhammad and Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father all from ibn Mahbub from ‘ Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajj aj who has said the following: “I once asked abu al-Hassan, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, about the case of a man who marries a woman secretly in the house of her family. He wants to divorce her but cannot reach her to know about her Hayd (menses) and does not know when she becomes clean of Hayd (menses). He (the Imam) said, ‘This is like the case of a husband who is absent who divorces by counting new moon and months.’

I then asked, ‘What happens if he is able to reach her at certain times to find out about her Hayd (menses): how he should divorce her?’ He (the Imam) said, ‘When a month, during which he is not able to reach her, passes he can divorce her when he finds himself in the beginning of the next month. He must write down about the month in which he has divorced and arrange for two men as witnesses. When three months pass she becomes stranger to him and he becomes one of those who can propose marriage. He, however, must pay her expenses for the three months in which she counted the waiting period.’”
